articles.title: ‘It’s greed’: Zohran Mamdani blasts Amazon over new $5 fee hike in NYC. Is your next order about to get pricier?
articles.summary: An express delivery straight against your bottom line.
articles.body:
Moneywise and Yahoo Finance LLC may earn commission or revenue through links in the content below.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is taking aim at Amazon over a warning the online retail giant has been flashing at New Yorkers as they shop: Their orders could soon cost as much as $5 more.

"Amazon is a multi-trillion dollar company. If Jeff Bezos adds $5 to your order, it's not because of City Council's efforts to protect workers' rights and keep our streets safe," Mamdani wrote in a Nov. 19 post on X (1). "It's greed."

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 5 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change

Gold has overtaken U.S. Treasuries as central banks' top reserve asset. Get Goldco's 2026 Precious Metals IRA Playbook for free

Amazon is fighting a proposed New York City law (2) that would overhaul how the company gets packages from its warehouses to your doorstep. And now the giant seems to be recruiting its own customers to help fight that legislative battle.

The company has begun displaying warnings on its website and in its shopping app, directing customers to contact their local lawmakers and oppose the legislation.

For Americans who have come to depend on the convenience of online shopping, the prospect of paying more every time they click "buy" is hardly welcome news. But how much of Amazon's warning should shoppers take at face value?

Why Amazon is threatening to raise prices

Introduced in February by New York City Councilwoman Tiffany Cabán, the Delivery Protection Act (3) would require companies operating certain delivery facilities to directly employ most of their warehouse and delivery workers rather than outsource those jobs to third-party contractors.

The legislation would also establish a $500 annual licensing fee per facility, mandatory worker safety training and additional protections against unfair dismissal.

Amazon contends that complying with the legislation could make its existing delivery model economically untenable in New York City, potentially forcing it to relocate operations beyond city limits.

The company has cited research from consulting firm AKRF estimating additional annual household costs of between $409 and $664. However, Amazon hasn't established precisely how those figures translate into a $5 increase per order, per Fox Business (4).

And the bill, which remains in committee, hasn't passed yet.

articles.title: What really happens when you need help restoring your identity
articles.summary: Identity theft restoration involves credit freezes, fraud alerts and disputing fraudulent records. Here's how the recovery process works, step by step.
articles.body: Identity theft restoration takes more than one phone call. It often means securing accounts, documenting fraudulent activity and working with several companies to correct inaccurate records. The term "identity restoration" can sound complicated until you suddenly need it. Maybe someone opened a credit card in your name, took over your bank account or used your personal information to get medical care. Now you're dealing with unfamiliar charges, paperwork and companies that all seem to have different requirements. Fortunately, knowing what happens during recovery can make the process easier to manage. Here's how identity restoration typically works, what you may need to do yourself and where professional help can make a difference. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. IDENTITY RESTORATION: WHAT TO DO AFTER IDENTITY THEFT 1. The first conversation establishes what happened Identity restoration usually starts with understanding the problem. A specialist may ask when you first noticed suspicious activity, which accounts someone accessed and whether you lost money or personal information. These details help identify the type of identity theft involved. Someone opening a credit card in your name requires a different response than a criminal taking over your phone number or using your medical information. A restoration specialist can help you separate confirmed fraud from suspicious activity that still needs investigation. As a result, you can focus on the companies and accounts that need attention first. 2. The immediate risk gets contained Before tackling paperwork, focus on preventing additional damage. Depending on what happened, you may need to contact your bank, lock a credit card, change passwords or secure your mobile phone account. If someone accessed your email, make securing that account an early priority. Criminals can use compromised email accounts to reset passwords and gain access to other services. You may also want to place a fraud alert or freeze your credit. Neither option fixes fraud that has already occurred. However, both can help reduce the risk of additional new-account fraud. 3. A case file helps keep everything organized One of the most frustrating parts of identity theft recovery is having to explain the same problem repeatedly. A case file helps you keep track of important information and avoid starting over with every phone call. Include dates of suspicious activity, copies of statements, confirmation numbers, correspondence and the names of representatives you've contacted. Also, record what each company promised to do and when you should expect a response. This becomes especially helpful when several organizations are involved. For example, your bank might close an account while a fraudulent balance still appears on your credit report. Having documentation gives you a clear record of the steps you've already completed. Keep those records somewhere secure. Additionally, avoid sending sensitive documents through unverified email addresses or links. 4. The appropriate institutions get involved Depending on the type of fraud, identity restoration may involve banks, creditors, credit bureaus, mobile carriers, medical providers or government agencies. Each organization follows its own procedures. A bank may ask you to complete a fraud affidavit, while a credit bureau may request an identity theft report before blocking fraudulent information. A restoration specialist can explain those requirements and help you navigate the process. In some situations, the specialist may also coordinate communications or work with institutions on your behalf. However, you may still need to verify your identity, provide documents or authorize certain actions. Restoration assistance helps you work through the process, but the affected institutions remain responsible for reviewing claims and correcting their records. 5. You dispute and correct fraudulent records Once you secure your accounts and identify the affected organizations, the next step involves correcting the damage. If someone opened a fraudulent credit account, you may need to dispute the information with the creditor and the credit bureaus. The Federal Trade Commission recommends reporting identity theft through IdentityTheft.gov, where you can create an FTC Identity Theft Report and receive a personalized recovery plan. An FTC Identity Theft Report can also help you exercise important rights, including requesting that credit bureaus block information resulting from identity theft. Medical identity theft may require contacting healthcare providers and insurers to correct inaccurate records. Meanwhile, tax identity theft generally involves working directly with the IRS. Keep copies of every document you submit. Whenever possible, request written confirmation after an organization resolves an issue. 6. Follow-ups continue until the problems are resolved Identity theft recovery rarely happens all at once. Your bank might reverse a fraudulent transaction before a credit bureau finishes investigating a related account. Similarly, a phone carrier may restore your number, but you may still need to strengthen account security to prevent another takeover. That's why follow-ups are so important. Set reminders for promised responses and continue checking your statements, accounts and credit reports after the initial incident. You can review your credit reports for free each week at AnnualCreditReport.com. Even after you resolve a case, additional suspicious activity can surface if criminals continue trying to use your stolen information. WAS YOUR IDENTITY STOLEN? WHAT TO DO IN THE FIRST 24 HOURS Recovery depends on the type of identity theft Not every identity theft case follows the same path. The type of fraud determines which organizations need to get involved and what steps you should take. For example, new-account fraud often involves creditors and credit bureaus. An existing bank-account takeover requires immediate attention from the financial institution, while medical identity theft may involve correcting treatment and billing records. Tax or government benefits fraud can require separate reporting procedures. And if a scammer convinced you to authorize a payment, your options may differ from those available for unauthorized account transactions. That's why identifying the problem early is important. A credit freeze may help protect against new credit accounts, but it cannot correct a medical record or recover money sent to a scammer. How to tell whether your recovery is progressing Identity theft recovery can feel slow, especially when you're waiting for several companies to respond. However, you can track progress by focusing on specific actions rather than expecting everything to happen immediately. Have you secured the compromised account? Did you report the fraudulent charge? Has the credit bureau acknowledged your dispute? Each completed step helps move the case forward. If a company misses a deadline or provides conflicting information, your case file will help you explain the situation without starting the conversation from scratch. What you may need to provide during restoration Before speaking with a restoration specialist or fraud department, gather any suspicious statements, letters, alerts or emails connected to the incident. The company may also ask you to provide identification, an FTC Identity Theft Report or written authorization allowing someone to assist with your case. Always verify that you're communicating with the legitimate organization before sharing sensitive information. Also, ask why a document is necessary and how the company plans to handle it. Ultimately, you should understand what information you're providing and what actions someone may take on your behalf. How an identity protection service can help with restoration If you've experienced identity theft, handling multiple disputes and follow-up calls yourself can become overwhelming. That's where an identity protection service may help. Some services provide access to identity restoration specialists who can guide you through the recovery process. Depending on the provider and your plan, specialists may help organize documentation, explain next steps and assist with communications involving affected institutions. Identity protection services may also monitor certain personal information, credit reports and financial accounts. Alerts can help you discover suspicious activity before it leads to additional problems. However, identity monitoring cannot detect every form of fraud, and restoration assistance cannot guarantee that every dispute will end in your favor. The benefit comes from having experienced support when you're trying to work through a complicated situation. Other identity protection tools that can support recovery Beyond restoration assistance, some identity protection services offer tools that help you identify suspicious activity, reduce the exposure of personal information and respond when something looks wrong. Features vary by provider and plan, so it's worth checking what's included before signing up. Review where your payment card information is stored Some services offer tools that help you identify merchants and websites that may have your payment card information on file. Reviewing these connections can help you decide where to remove stored payment details, especially if you no longer use certain accounts. However, these tools cannot automatically confirm whether someone has stolen your card information. Unexpected and suspicious charge alerts Certain identity protection services can monitor eligible financial accounts and flag transactions that appear unusual or potentially fraudulent. These might include unfamiliar purchases or unexpected charges. An alert gives you an opportunity to review the transaction and contact your financial institution if necessary. Keep in mind that these services may not detect every suspicious transaction. Personal data removal services Some identity protection services include tools that search covered data broker websites for your personal information and submit removal requests on your behalf. Reducing publicly available information may help limit your exposure to identity theft and scams. However, no removal service can erase your information from every website or guarantee that it will never reappear. Scam assistance and identity protection guidance Some providers offer access to support specialists or online tools that can help you evaluate suspicious messages, websites and financial activity. Depending on the service, you may receive guidance on reporting scams, securing accounts and taking steps to recover from identity theft. Certain plans may also include reimbursement benefits for eligible losses or expenses, subject to coverage limits and exclusions. However, these services cannot guarantee that you'll recover money you sent to a scammer. Always review the terms before relying on a particular benefit. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at Cyberguy.com Kurt's key takeaways When someone steals your identity, discovering the fraud is often only the beginning. The real work comes afterward, when you're trying to secure accounts, correct records and get answers from companies handling different parts of the problem. I've always believed that knowing what to do next can make a stressful situation much easier to handle. Start by protecting the accounts you still control, document everything and use the free recovery tools available through the FTC. If you want additional help, an identity protection service with restoration specialists may help you navigate the recovery process and stay organized. No service can promise an instant fix, but having experienced support can make a difference when you're dealing with identity theft.
